title: Puiseux's Theorem: Wiedijk #41
content:
**Puiseux's Theorem**:

The field of Puiseux series K{{x}} over an algebraically closed field K of characteristic 0 is **algebraically closed**.

**Puiseux Series**: Fractional power series
$$f(x) = \sum_{n \geq n_0} a_n \cdot x^{n/m}$$
where m is the ramification index.

**Examples**:
- √x = x^{1/2} (ramification 2)
- 1 + x^{1/3} + x^{2/3} + ... (ramification 3)
- x^{-1/2} + 1 + x^{1/2} + ... (negative exponents allowed)

**Historical**: Newton (1676) discovered the algorithm; Puiseux (1850) gave the first rigorous proof. The theorem provides the most explicit algebraic closure in mathematics — roots are not merely shown to exist, but can be algorithmically computed via the Newton polygon.
mathContext: K{{x}} = ⋃_{n≥1} K((x^{1/n})) is algebraically closed when K is algebraically closed and char(K) = 0. Equivalently: K{{x}} = algebraic closure of K((x)).

crossReferences.relationship: FTA shows ℂ is algebraically closed; Puiseux shows ℂ{{x}} is also algebraically closed — extending the result from constants to power series
Abel-Ruffini shows degree ≥ 5 polynomials over ℚ have no radical formula; Puiseux series provide an alternative solution format over Laurent series

prerequisites: formal power series and Laurent series

title: Puiseux Series via Hahn Series
content:
**Puiseux Series Definition**:

A Hahn series f ∈ HahnSeries ℚ K is a Puiseux series if its exponents have a **common denominator**:

$$\exists n \in \mathbb{N}^+: \text{supp}(f) \subseteq \frac{1}{n}\mathbb{Z}$$

In Lean: `IsPuiseuxSeries f := ∃ n : ℕ+, ∀ q ∈ f.support, ∃ k : ℤ, q = k / n`

Mathlib's `HahnSeries Γ R` provides generalized power series with well-ordered support over a linearly ordered group Γ. Puiseux series are the subring where Γ = ℚ and support lies in (1/n)ℤ.

**Key property**: The union ⋃_{n≥1} K((x^{1/n})) over all ramification indices forms the full Puiseux series field. Each K((x^{1/n})) is a finite extension of K((x)) of degree n.
mathContext: IsPuiseuxSeries(f) ⟺ ∃n ∈ ℕ⁺, supp(f) ⊆ (1/n)ℤ. The field K{{x}} = colim_n K((x^{1/n})) = ⋃_{n≥1} K((x^{1/n})). Each K((x^{1/n}))/K((x)) is a totally ramified extension of degree n.
prerequisites: the ramification index n in x^{1/n}

title: Algebraic Closure Theorem
content:
**Main Theorem** (axiomatized):

For K algebraically closed of characteristic 0:
$$K\{\{x\}\} = \overline{K((x))}$$

Puiseux series form the algebraic closure of Laurent series.

**Two axiomatized statements**:
1. `puiseux_theorem`: every polynomial over K of positive degree has Puiseux series coefficients forming a root
2. `puiseux_is_algebraic_closure`: every polynomial specified by degree and coefficients has a root with explicit ramification index

**Why axiomatized**: A complete proof requires rigorous treatment of Puiseux series arithmetic, Newton polygon construction, convergence of the Newton-Puiseux iteration, and the delicate characteristic 0 argument. This is ~2000+ lines of infrastructure.
mathContext: axiom: ∀K alg. closed, char 0, ∀P ∈ K[Y] with deg(P) > 0, ∃ Puiseux series y s.t. P(y) = 0. Equivalently: K{{x}} is algebraically closed.

crossReferences.relationship: FTA proves ℂ = algebraic closure of ℝ; Puiseux proves ℂ{{x}} = algebraic closure of ℂ((x)) — both are explicit algebraic closure results

prerequisites: the field of Laurent series over ℂ

title: Newton-Puiseux Algorithm
content:
**Constructive Root Finding**:

**Input**: Monic polynomial P(Y) ∈ K{{x}}[Y] of degree n
**Output**: n Puiseux series roots

**Algorithm**:
1. **Newton Polygon**: Lower convex hull of {(i, ord(aᵢ)) : aᵢ ≠ 0} where P(Y) = Σᵢ aᵢ(x)Yⁱ
2. **Edge Analysis**: Edge with slope −p/q (in lowest terms) → leading exponent p/q
3. **Characteristic Polynomial**: Restrict to points on the edge; roots c of this polynomial give leading coefficients
4. **Substitution**: Y = c·x^{p/q}(1 + Y'), get simpler polynomial P'(Y')
5. **Recurse**: Apply algorithm to P' for higher-order terms
6. **Termination**: Newton polygon strictly improves at each step (key argument uses char 0)

**Example** (Y² = x): Newton polygon edge from (0,1) to (2,0), slope −1/2, characteristic poly c² = 1, solutions Y = ±x^{1/2}.

The constructive nature is what makes Puiseux's theorem so powerful: roots are not just shown to exist but can be computed to any desired precision.
mathContext: Newton polygon Γ(P) = lower convex hull of {(i, v(aᵢ))}. Edge of slope −p/q contributes roots with leading term c·x^{p/q}. The multiplicity of the edge = number of roots contributed.

crossReferences.relationship: Cardano's formula gives explicit roots of cubics over ℚ; Newton-Puiseux gives explicit series roots of all polynomials over K((x))

prerequisites: the Newton polygon and its lower convex hull

title: Applications: Curve Singularities and Tropical Geometry
content:
**Resolution of Curve Singularities**:

Near a singular point of f(x,y) = 0, each **branch** of the curve is parameterized by a Puiseux series y = Σ aₙ x^{n/m}.

**Examples**:
- **Cusp** y² = x³: single branch y = ±x^{3/2}, ramification 2
- **Node** y² = x²(x+1): two branches y = ±x·√(x+1) = ±x(1 + x/2 − x²/8 + ...)
- **Tacnode** y² = x⁴: two tangent branches y = ±x²

**Algebraic Functions**: Multi-valued functions y(x) from P(x,y) = 0 become single-valued as Puiseux series on sectors of the complex plane. Monodromy around the branch point permutes the series.

**Tropical Connection**: Newton polygon slopes correspond to tropical roots — the valuations of the algebraic roots. This provides the foundational link between classical algebraic geometry and tropical geometry.
mathContext: For f(x,y) = 0 with singularity at origin: branches ↔ irreducible factors of f in K{{x}}[y]. Puiseux expansion yᵢ(x) = Σ aₙ x^{n/mᵢ} parameterizes the ith branch. Intersection multiplicity = Σ v(yᵢ − yⱼ).

title: Galois Group: Profinite Integers
content:
**Galois Theory of the Puiseux Extension**:

$$\text{Gal}(K\{\{x\}\} / K((x))) \cong \hat{\mathbb{Z}}$$

where Ẑ = lim←_n ℤ/nℤ is the profinite completion of ℤ.

**Galois Action**: An automorphism σ ∈ Gal is determined by a compatible system (σₙ)_{n≥1} where σₙ: x^{1/n} ↦ ζₙ^{kₙ} · x^{1/n} with ζₙ a primitive nth root of unity, and kₘ ≡ kₙ (mod n) whenever n | m.

**Significance**:
- The profinite integers Ẑ ≅ ∏_p ℤ_p (product over all primes) is an uncountable group
- This is a key example in infinite Galois theory
- The extension is the union of all finite cyclic extensions K((x^{1/n}))/K((x))
- Relates to the fundamental group of the punctured disk π₁(𝔻 \ {0}) ≅ Ẑ
mathContext: Gal(K{{x}}/K((x))) ≅ Ẑ = lim←_n ℤ/nℤ ≅ ∏_p ℤ_p. Action: σ(x^{1/n}) = ζₙ^k · x^{1/n}. Subgroup of index n: Gal(K{{x}}/K((x^{1/n}))) ≅ nẐ.

crossReferences.relationship: De Moivre's theorem gives nth roots of unity ζₙ = e^{2πi/n}; these roots of unity generate the Galois action on Puiseux series

title: Concrete Calculations
content:
**Worked Examples**:

| Equation | Newton Polygon | Slope | Puiseux Root |
|----------|---------------|-------|--------------|
| Y² = x | (0,1)→(2,0) | −1/2 | ±x^{1/2} |
| Y² = x³ (cusp) | (0,3)→(2,0) | −3/2 | ±x^{3/2} |
| Y³ = x | (0,1)→(3,0) | −1/3 | ω^k x^{1/3}, k=0,1,2 |
| Y² − Y = x^{−1} | Two edges | varies | Laurent + fractional parts |

The formalization verifies specific exponents: `square_root_puiseux` confirms exponent 1/2 for Y² = x, and `cusp_parameterization` confirms exponent 3/2 for the cusp Y² = x³.

These examples illustrate how the Newton polygon method systematically determines leading exponents, after which the characteristic polynomial determines leading coefficients and recursion computes higher-order terms.
mathContext: Y² = x: Newton polygon slope = −(1−0)/(2−0) = −1/2, char poly c² − 1 = 0, roots c = ±1. Y² = x³: slope = −3/2, exponent = 3/2.

title: Analogy with p-adic Numbers: Hensel's Lemma
content:
**p-adic Analogy**: Puiseux's theorem has a striking parallel with p-adic algebraic closure:

| Puiseux (power series) | p-adic (number theory) |
|------------------------|------------------------|
| K((x)) (Laurent series) | ℚ_p (p-adic numbers) |
| K{{x}} (Puiseux series) | Q̄_p (algebraic closure) |
| x^{1/n} (fractional powers) | p^{1/n}, roots of unity |
| Newton polygon | Newton polygon (p-adic) |
| Ramification: x ↦ x^{1/n} | Ramification: totally ramified ext. |

**Hensel's Lemma** is the p-adic analogue of Newton-Puiseux: it lifts approximate roots to exact roots in complete valued fields.

Both are instances of a general pattern: **algebraic closure of a complete discretely-valued field** requires adjoining roots of the uniformizer and roots of unity. In characteristic 0, these suffice (Puiseux); in characteristic p, Artin-Schreier extensions are also needed.
mathContext: K((x)) is a complete discretely-valued field with uniformizer x and residue field K. Its maximal unramified extension: K((x)) (already alg. closed residue). Its algebraic closure: K{{x}} = ⋃_n K((x^{1/n})).

title: Characteristic Zero Requirement
content:
**Puiseux Fails in Positive Characteristic!**

**Counterexample**: Over 𝔽_p((x)), the Artin-Schreier polynomial:
$$Y^p - Y - x^{-1} = 0$$
has no solution in any K((x^{1/n})), hence no Puiseux series root.

**Why**: In characteristic p, there are two types of field extensions:
- **Ramified**: Y^n = x (these work like char 0, give Puiseux-type roots)
- **Artin-Schreier**: Y^p − Y = f(x) (these are inseparable at the wild level and cannot be expressed via fractional powers)

The algebraic closure of 𝔽_p((x)) requires infinitely many Artin-Schreier extensions stacked on top of each other — a fundamentally different structure from the Puiseux tower.

This is why `CharZero K` appears as a hypothesis in the formalization.
mathContext: char(K) = p > 0 ⟹ K{{x}} ≠ algebraic closure of K((x)). Artin-Schreier: Yᵖ − Y = f generates degree-p extensions not contained in any K((x^{1/n})). Wild ramification index divisible by p causes failure.

title: Mathematical Significance
content:
**Bridges Three Areas of Mathematics**:

1. **Algebra**: Provides a concrete, explicit algebraic closure K{{x}} with computable Galois group Ẑ. Unlike most algebraic closures (constructed via Zorn's lemma), this one comes with an algorithm.

2. **Analysis**: Local expansions near singularities converge (for K = ℂ) in a neighborhood of the branch point. The convergent Puiseux series suffice for studying algebraic curves analytically.

3. **Geometry**: Foundation for resolution of curve singularities — every branch of an algebraic curve at a singular point is parameterized by a convergent Puiseux series. This is the starting point of singularity theory.

**Modern applications**:
- **Computer algebra**: Symbolic root-finding algorithms (Maple, Mathematica)
- **Tropical geometry**: Newton polygon = tropicalization of the polynomial
- **Arithmetic geometry**: Local analysis of algebraic varieties over complete fields
mathContext: K{{x}} is the unique (up to isomorphism) algebraic closure of K((x)) when char(K) = 0. It is the maximal totally ramified extension of K((x)) when K is already algebraically closed.

crossReferences.relationship: Vieta's formulas relate polynomial coefficients to symmetric functions of roots; for Puiseux roots, these become identities in the Puiseux series field
